entries.title: China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
entries.summary: The US and China agree that advanced AI poses serious risks. But Beijing is deeply skeptical of a deal that prioritizes keeping US companies ahead.
entries.content:
For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China, and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous, tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down.

“Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier.”

China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don't believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal.

“The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it's being treated from a position of equals."

Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies.

“His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI. “Which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.”

Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”)

The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained.

When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fear-mongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.”

The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power.

“Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value partly because it’s skeptical of the possibility of achieving AGI and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity,” says Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security focused on national security and artificial intelligence. “Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.”

In a recent essay, China’s minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest, and new military threats. He spent far less time on the kinds of doomsday scenarios that frequently preoccupy people at US frontier AI labs.

“Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls for AI safety as instrumental,” says Nie. “They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.”

That skepticism is also shared by many people who work in China’s AI industry, which has broadly focused on releasing lower-cost, open-weight models. In a widely shared essay published on Sunday, a researcher at DeepSeek said he believes AI could move human society to one of two extremes. In the first, powerful AI is broadly available and raises living standards. In the second, a handful of tech companies control the most advanced systems and the resources that come with them, making it even harder for everyone else to catch up.

“That is why I still believe the most advanced intelligence should be made available to everyone in an open and inexpensive way,” the DeepSeek engineer wrote. “I do not trust Anthropic or OpenAI to do that. And I especially do not want Anthropic to control the most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI.”

None of this means that US-China cooperation on AI safety is doomed. Preliminary negotiations between the two countries are reportedly already underway ahead of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s planned visit to Washington later this month to meet with US President Donald Trump.

There are plenty of reasons to be hopeful that these discussions will result in some progress, even though it may be incremental. Both governments have expressed worries about some of the same things, including cybersecurity threats, the misuse of powerful models, and the possibility that increasingly capable AI systems could behave in unexpected ways.

“There are people who genuinely care about AI safety on both sides, and there’s a possibility they could engage in good-faith discussion in narrowly scoped issues,” says Nie. What might move the needle most, she says, is designing a credible way for each country to verify that the other is abiding by its commitments.

Still, others worry that rhetoric from Amodei and other US tech leaders about weakening China could erode the fragile trust that diplomatic talks depend on. Kristy Loke, a research fellow at the AI safety nonprofit MATS Research, says that Amodei’s missive may ultimately backfire. “Dario is undermining one of the few available levers for reducing the very risks he professes to take seriously,” she says.

entries.title: Why It Seems Like Great White Sharks Are Overrunning Maine
entries.summary: While a bunch of sharks cruising the Maine coast may seem ominous, it’s actually a sign of a conservation success story.
entries.content:
Lifeguard Greg Wilfert was swimming off the coast of Scarborough, Maine, in August when he was yanked underwater by a force tugging on his rescue buoy. Wilfert, a lifeguard of 55 years, told local news outlet WFSB that he first thought he’d gotten caught on a boat propeller, but the real culprit was a great white shark.

The incident is one in a long line of great white sightings off the coast of Maine this year. It was a busy summer for shark sightings along the rest of the East Coast, but Maine, in particular, seems to have had a great white bonanza. A dozen sightings were reported in a two-day period near Pine Point Beach in southern Maine in August. Beaches were temporarily closed all over the state following multiple sightings throughout July and August. The sharks followed beachgoers through the end of summer: A great white was spotted off Wells Beach over Labor Day weekend, while a fisherman caught another on the holiday about 30 miles down the coast.

The waters off the coast of Maine are some of the world’s fastest-warming, and the Atlantic has seen a series of marine heat waves. The El Niño weather phenomenon is only boosting global heat further. But experts told WIRED that the reason for our recent glut of shark encounters is a lot more complicated than just attributing them to climate change, especially when it comes to great whites. Instead, a successful conservation effort decades ago is likely starting to pay dividends, coupled with more people bringing technology that can spot sharks to the beach.

When Steven Spielberg’s classic movie Jaws came out in 1975, great whites were in trouble. The species had declined in waters off both the east and west coasts of the US thanks to overfishing, bycatch, and trophy hunting. In the 1990s, federal protections were instated for both the sharks and for gray seals, one of their key prey species.

Maine’s state shark monitoring system uses a technology called acoustic telemetry, which outfits the animal with a tag that emits a unique electronic signature. Underwater stations can then pick up on that signal and log the tagged sharks, helping track their movement up and down the coast. Maine’s program is less than a decade old, and “not every shark is tagged,” says Matthew Davis, a shark expert at Maine’s Department of Natural Resources. That makes pinpointing exactly what is going on with this uptick in sightings a little more challenging.

But Davis and Walter Golet, an associate professor at the University of Maine School of Marine Science who collaborates on shark research, both believe that there were more great whites off the coast this summer compared to decades past. They attribute it in part to federal protections working. Great whites males take 26 years to reach adulthood, while females can take up to 33 years. That timeframe aligns with when federal protections were put in place and could help explain why more sharks are showing up off of Maine. Research generally backs this up: Multiple studies have found that protections for both sharks and seals helped to increase populations along the East Coast.

While climate change has driven massive changes in the ocean, including pushing many species northward as waters warm, its direct effect on great white sharks is a little more murky. Some research has suggested that great whites could suffer from very hot ocean temperatures by causing them to overheat and forcing them to slow down or move to colder water to seek food. But James Sulikowski, the director of the Coastal Oregon Marine Experiment Station at Oregon State University, emphasizes that great whites can control their body temperature, which enables them to withstand much larger ranges in ocean temperatures than other shark species.

“They’re not so subject to these huge fluctuations—they’re really good regulators,” he says.

Davis says that the knock-on effects of climate change—like warmer ocean temperatures changing certain prey species’ habitat range—are more likely to impact great whites than the hotter ocean temperatures do. Prey species may “hang around a little bit longer because the water is going to be a little bit warmer,” he says, which could mean great whites spend more time in areas they previously would’ve been in for only a few months.

Another indirect impact of climate change: more people at the beach during hot days. And, since it’s 2026, more and more people bring equipment, from iPhones to hobby drones, that can capture high-quality footage of marine life. All three experts say that the raft of shark sightings in Maine this summer may just be a result of people going outside with better, more technologically advanced eyes on the ocean.

“There are more of them, but they are also easier to see, so you have to untangle that,” says Golet. “I think we’re all sort of a prisoner of our own timeline.”

entries.title: Best 2-in-1 Laptops (2026): Microsoft, Lenovo, and the iPad
entries.summary: These portable computers balance tablet and laptop functionality, whether you want a screen that detaches or spins.
entries.content:
There will always be a use case for owning both a laptop and a tablet as stand-alone products. But the 2-in-1 laptop is the utopian dream of combining these two into a single device.

Of all the models I've tested, no 2-in-1 laptop is equally good at being both a tablet and a laptop. They always lean toward one or the other. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't buy one, especially since the convenience of having both in one device makes it an easier pill to swallow, price-wise.

The products below should meet most people’s needs. But if none are a fit for you, check out WIRED's other computer buying guides, including the Best Laptops, Best Surface Devices, Best Cheap Laptops, the Best Tablets, and the Best iPad.

Updated September 2026: I've made the Surface Pro 12 my new top pick and rearranged many of the other recommendations on my list.

The Best Detachable 2-in-1 Tablets

You can't talk about 2-in-1 laptops without talking about Microsoft's Surface devices. These tablets have removable keyboards that attach magnetically, not unlike an iPad. This form factor lets you switch between tablet and laptop modes. It's just as functional as a tablet as it is as a laptop. As I said, the Surface Pro is the epitome of this design, pioneering the idea of a tablet with a built-in kickstand that runs a full version of Windows.

The best model to buy right now is the Surface Pro 12 (6/10, WIRED Reviewed). The smaller screen and compact design befit a 2-in-1 tablet that's meant to be held in one hand (at least occasionally). This wasn't my favorite when it came out, largely because it was overpriced at the time. But with all the configuration changes and price increases in the Surface Pro lineup, this model has become my go-to recommendation.

This is the most successful small tablet Microsoft has ever made, and a big reason is that it doesn't cheap out on quality or shrink down the size too much. With a 12-inch screen, it still allows the keyboard to be large enough to type on comfortably. It doesn't have the option for an OLED screen, but the device still feels surprisingly premium, and it is even more portable than its older sibling.

Not only is the Surface Pro 12 cheaper overall, but it's also the only 256-GB storage model on offer, which gives you a more affordable starting configuration. Regardless, you get the Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus, which gives the Surface Pro 12 excellent battery life and solid performance. And because Surface devices run a full version of Windows, they are the best 2-in-1 options to use as full laptop replacements. But be careful: Microsoft sells a $750 starting configuration with only 8 GB of RAM, which may limit multitasking and heavier applications.

An even better laptop replacement, however, is the Surface Pro 13.8 (7/10, WIRED Recommends). The larger screen gives you more visual real estate, and the larger touchpad on the keyboard cover is more comfortable to use. The keyboard cover also comes with fabric-like textured palm rests and a built-in spot to hold the Surface Slim Pen 2. I also like the option to upgrade to an OLED screen, which makes it a more capable iPad Pro competitor. The only problem is that price increases have made this larger Surface Pro feel overpriced. The 2026 Snapdragon X2 Elite or X2 Plus models have largely replaced the 2024 model I tested, priced at $1,600. For me, that's too expensive for something meant to be more of a compact travel device. That's especially true since you still have to buy the keyboard cover. That's why I'd recommend this older Snapdragon X Elite model, which gets you the OLED display with a 120-Hz refresh rate and also bundles in the keyboard and stylus. On top of that, it even includes a terabyte of storage. That's well worth it.

While the hardware makes for a good tablet, Windows still isn't a very touch-friendly operating system and lacks a touch-first app ecosystem to support it. That's where iPads come into play. The iPad Air and iPad Pro are the best tablets you can buy, largely thanks to the breadth of touch-first apps available in the App Store. In many ways, that's what makes an iPad such an ideal 2-in-1 laptop, especially if you actually want to use it as a tablet. They are also easier to hold in one hand because they are lighter than Surface devices. These days, iPads are increasingly becoming legitimate laptop replacements too. With the Magic Keyboard attachment, you can add an additional USB-C port and a full-size keyboard and trackpad. I also like that this design doesn't rely on a kickstand, which makes it easier to use on your lap than the Surface.

While iPadOS isn't perfect, the introduction of windowing and improved cursor support over the years have made iPads work more like laptops than ever. But which iPad should you buy? The latest model I tested, the M4 iPad Air, is immensely powerful, and with the Magic Keyboard attached, it's a solid 2-in-1 laptop that costs less than the Surface Pro with the keyboard included. It's plenty of performance for just about anything you'd want to do with an iPad, especially if you opt for the larger 13-inch model. My only real complaint is that the palm rests on the Magic Keyboard are quite small.

Lastly, I have to point to the Asus ROG Flow Z13, one of the most interesting detachable 2-in-1s. I don't know anyone who has asked for a gaming-based 2-in-1, but Asus went out and made one anyway that actually works. Although you likely won't use the ROG Flow Z13 much as a tablet, the form factor keeps heat away from your hands. Unlike almost every other portable gaming device you can buy, your hands on the keyboard stay cool and sweat-free. This 2025 model is still a good buy, since only a more expensive, special-edition version came out in 2026.

The Best Convertible 2-in-1 Laptops

A different breed of 2-in-1 is commonly called a convertible laptop. These look like traditional laptops, but they have two unique features: a 360-degree hinge that allows the screen to flip to the back of the device, and a touchscreen. Most often, people enjoy tilting the screen back and laying the keyboard upside down on the table to watch movies and videos. You can go into tablet mode by folding the screen all the way back against the bottom screen, but the thickness and weight of these devices make it fairly uncomfortable to use that way.

I'll admit these aren't my favorite laptop designs. While I appreciate a touchscreen, I rarely use the 360-degree hinge in these other poses, not to mention downsides like a wobbly screen, an unattractive hinge, and extra cost. Lenovo, however, has made a name for itself in this category with its Yoga line, creating the very best of this look (though even Lenovo has begun launching “Yoga Slim” models that ditch the 2-in-1 aspect). That aside, I really enjoyed the Lenovo Yoga 9i that I reviewed in 2025.

The 2026 version, the Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition, is largely the same laptop, except with a newer Intel Core Ultra 7 355 processor. Bar none, this is one of the most premium laptops you can buy, sporting a classy design, a very sharp OLED screen, and a thin chassis. One interesting aspect of this design is that Lenovo added an extra benefit to the 360-hinge by building a loudspeaker into it that delivers higher-quality audio, regardless of the mode you're using it in.

The other convertible 2-in-1 I'd point you to is the Framework Laptop 12 (7/10, WIRED Recommends). I'm a big fan of Framework devices because of their great repairability, which lets you replace or upgrade nearly every internal component. You can even upgrade the processor and motherboard, which Framework sells separately. In theory, that means more years of use and less e-waste. Admittedly, it has a fairly thick chassis. But it's affordable, and the 2-in-1 hinge makes it a great, versatile family or student computer. To save money, you can opt for the DIY Edition, which requires assembling the laptop from its components. Framework's elegant, well-documented system makes the building process much more enjoyable than you might think. It would also make for a fun education project for a kid.

I've also tested many convertible Chromebooks over the years, but my favorite is the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. Not only is this the best 2-in-1 Chromebook, it's also the best 2-in-1 you can buy for under $600. It uses a powerful (and efficient) chip from MediaTek that gives it competitive battery life, something Chromebooks have lacked for years now. It even comes with a higher-resolution screen and 12 GB of RAM; it's pretty stacked for a Chromebook. Googlebooks are coming soon to take the baton from Chromebooks, but for now, the selection of 2-in-1 Chromebooks is dwindling. Hopefully, we'll see a surge of interest in Googlebooks that brings more 2-in-1 laptops to market.

Other 2-in-1 Laptops to Consider

Lenovo Chromebook Duet Gen 9 for $259: The Lenovo Chromebook Duet Gen 9 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) was one of my favorite pieces of tech when it came out for one reason: its size. This diminutive detachable laptop is only 11 inches, which sounds painful at first. But this isn’t a productivity machine. Rather, it’s better viewed as a companion you can take anywhere for light web browsing, writing, and watching videos.

Lenovo Flex 5i Chromebook Plus for $630: We’ve long been fans of the Lenovo Flex 5i Chromebook Plus (8/10, WIRED Recommends), though it's beginning to show its age next to newer models. This one used to sell for as low as $500, which made it a solid budget alternative to the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 mentioned above, but these days the prices are on par. The Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 is better on every front, though, so depending on the current discount, I’d recommend that one over the older Flex 5i.

Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 for $750: You might think a 16-inch 2-in-1 laptop sounds silly. It's not portable enough to use as a tablet, that's for sure. But if you need a large touchscreen on your laptop, there's reason to pick up something like the Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 (6/10, WIRED Review). The flexibility of having a 360-degree hinge is useful in all sorts of scenarios. This 16-inch 2-in-1 balances price, portability, and performance with just enough finesse to be worth it—but only consider it when on sale.

Asus ProArt PZ13 for $1,250: Another detachable, the Asus ProArt PZ13 (6/10, WIRED Recommends) takes inspiration from Microsoft’s Surface Pro 13 design at a much more affordable price. For $1,250, you get a detachable 2-in-1 that can go up to around 19 hours on a single charge—and importantly, the keyboard comes bundled. Unfortunately, the performance leaves much to be desired, and its three-piece design is confounding. Still, it’s a nice alternative to the 13-inch Surface Pro if you’re dead set on the style.

What Is a 2-in-1 Laptop?

A 2-in-1 is a laptop that can go from a standard clamshell laptop configuration to a tablet setup. Two main designs fall into this category: detachable tablets and convertible laptops.

Detachable tablets are Windows tablets meant to be used with magnetic keyboards, not unlike an iPad Pro. These let you completely separate the screen from the keyboard, using a kickstand on the back of the display to keep it upright. Microsoft’s Surface lineup popularized this design, and it's still going strong more than a decade after its introduction. We’re even starting to see dual-screen laptops arrive, adding even more flexibility (if you have the cash to spare). The main benefit of the detachable 2-in-1 is the portability. While they aren't as good to use on your lap, they are thinner and lighter, making them better stand-alone tablets and travel devices.

Laptops with convertible displays, on the other hand, use a 360-degree hinge that can position the screen flat, in “tent” mode, or flush against the laptop's underside. Think of this as a touchscreen clamshell laptop with a fancy rotating hinge. This flexibility makes them great for everything from signing documents to streaming TV shows and movies—and you can switch back to a standard laptop orientation when it’s time to work.

Should You Buy a 2-in-1 Laptop?

The big draw of 2-in-1 laptops is that they can be used as both a laptop and a tablet. While in laptop mode, they’re generally comparable to any other clamshell laptop you’ll find. However, Windows and ChromeOS aren’t exactly the best touch-oriented operating systems out there, so you may find the touchscreen experience lacking when using it as a pure tablet.

If you already use a recent iPad or Android tablet regularly, you may not get as much out of a 2-in-1. But if you don't, these 2-in-1 laptops can give you the functionality of both devices in one—hence the name. Beyond that, convertible laptops use 360-degree hinges to offer even more capabilities, such as flipping the laptop upside down in various modes.

The only real downside to choosing a convertible 2-in-1 over a clamshell is the design tweaks needed to incorporate the hinge. Sometimes the weight balance can feel off, and the heftier hinge can look ugly and sometimes require a larger bottom bezel under the display. They're often more expensive too.

Why Not Just Buy an iPad?

It's a good question. All in all, it remains difficult to beat the iPad or iPad Pro for pure tablet use. From a software and third-party app perspective, iPadOS is far more robust without a keyboard, though that may change with Apple's multitasking improvements in iPadOS 26.

Windows tablets are the opposite, benefiting from the full Windows 11 experience. That means you can get all your work done, in theory, on one device, while still having something highly mobile. Some people can even do all their work on an iPad Pro, for example, but others prefer (or require) a desktop computing environment such as macOS or Windows.

I still wish Microsoft would improve Windows' touch experience, though, which would make 2-in-1 laptops much more enticing than iPads.

How I Test

I test 2-in-1s much like how I test clamshell laptops. Before you add in the 2-in-1 element, laptops are already incredibly complex devices, and I test every possible aspect of them. That means I measure display quality, benchmark CPU speed, run it until the battery dies, and type on the keyboard—a lot.

With 2-in-1 laptops, though, there's more of a physical element that needs testing. If it's a detachable, I extend the kickstand and use it in a variety of scenarios. How does it balance on your lap? What's the adjustability of the angle of the kickstand? If it's a convertible 2-in-1, does the touchscreen feel responsive? Does the screen wobble like crazy when you tap it? These are questions only hands-on time with the 2-in-1 laptop can answer.

All the products I recommend were provided by the manufacturers. However, our opinions and test results are completely independent. I don't guarantee positive coverage (or coverage at all) when I agree to accept a review unit from a company. I often send units back once I'm done testing unless I need to do long-term testing.

entries.title: Polymarket’s Next Bet? It Can Also Be a Media Company
entries.summary: The legal battle over whether prediction markets are a form of gambling has overshadowed something else entirely: They’re already a new form of media.
entries.content:
Every day, a newsletter from the prediction market Polymarket hits my inbox with a subject line that could easily come from any number of politics-focused newspapers or magazines. Recent entries include “Houthis Reveal New Precision Strike Capabilities,” “BREAKING: Trump Unveils Green Energy Beam,” and “World War I, 2.0?”

These dispatches are roundups with breathless summaries of the day’s top stories, linking out to corresponding Polymarket markets—yes, this thing will happen; no, it won’t. As far as business news analysis goes, the newsletter is not exactly Bloomberg’s Money Stuff, or even Emily Sundberg’s Feed Me—but it’s recognizably a commercial editorial product, and one that plays an important role in the prediction market ecosystem.

The industry is currently embroiled in a series of legal battles over whether prediction markets are financial services (the view held by the markets and the federal government) or gambling platforms (the position of many state authorities and regulators). The fight over what kind of companies these are could end up in the Supreme Court, but in the meantime, both Polymarket and its even-more-popular archrival, Kalshi, have successfully positioned themselves as new media organizations too. For two companies associated with risk, it’s a notably old-school hedge.

All kinds of tech startups have launched editorial projects—did you know the alternative dating app Feeld has a surprisingly good magazine?—but the leading prediction markets are entrenching themselves into the mainstream media apparatus in a particularly aggressive way. A recent report noted that they’re integrated into a quarter of the top 20 companies listed in the S&P 500’s Communications Services sector. Polymarket has partnerships with Dow Jones and Substack, while Kalshi has deals with CNN, CNBC, and Fox Corp.

None of the agreements facilitate trading. Instead, they’re mainly about data sharing; news outlets want to know what people are putting their money on, and prediction markets are happy to oblige. The deals showcase prediction markets as information channels—places to go to find out about what’s happening. They’ve given Polymarket and Kalshi much-needed boosts in credibility and offered a straightforward introduction to the wider public. Prediction market boosters hype these products as “truth machines,” revealing public sentiment more accurately than polling or traditional reporting; when media outlets decide the odds themselves are newsworthy, they reinforce that message.

“Given the forecasting success of the markets, it's clear there is informational value,” says Kalshi spokesperson Jack Such. “And three out of four users don't trade, which suggests the informational use case is popular enough to be taken very seriously.” (Polymarket declined to comment.)

Providing data is only a small part of how these companies function as new media entities. On social media, their official accounts post like news outlets, adopting a vernacular that mashes up PopCrave’s frenzied sensibility with Bloomberg’s coverage areas. (The efforts haven’t been wholly reliable: A New York Times analysis earlier this year found that Polymarket’s newsy social accounts have published “false and misleading information.”)

Chief executive and founder Shayne Coplan has referred to the company’s partnership with X as “News 2.0.” In 2024, the company hinted at even more expansive ambitions, recruiting for an editor in chief role to lead “content and data journalism” efforts. It never made that hire, although political analyst and media founder Nate Silver came on later that year as an adviser. But on its careers page, the company beckons prospective employees by playing this angle up: “Become the new front page of the internet.”

Kalshi is less inclined to describe itself this way. When asked if it considered itself a media company, Such, the spokesperson, tells WIRED that it does not, though the markets themselves have “quasi-media” attributes because they follow the news. “We see ourselves as a financial exchange,” he says.

Sure. But why not both? Financial services companies have jumped into the media sector before, most obviously Bloomberg, which initially focused on providing market data and financial analytics before expanding to include journalism products. More recently, the online trading hub Robinhood—now also a Polymarket competitor with its own prediction market offerings—ran a media subsidiary called Sherwood before winding it down earlier this summer. Then there’s Hunterbook, which operates both an investigative outlet called Hunterbook News and a hedge fund that executes trades based on its outlet’s investigations.

Polymarket doesn’t have a dedicated subsidiary or editorial arm. But it has launched a weekly podcast called What Are the Odds? in partnership with the podcast network Dear Media. It stars a rotating cast of hosts known for celebrity news content, including podcasters and cocktail entrepreneurs Claudia and Jackie Oshry, the daughters of a prominent anti-Muslim activist.

It has also partnered with a prediction-markets-focused media startup called Eventual, which raised money from venture capital firms like Lightshed Capital as well as serial media entrepreneur and Bustle Digital Group owner Bryan Goldberg, who was also an early investor in Polymarket itself. “Polymarket's role in shaping media narratives was always a big piece of the puzzle,” Goldberg, who is best known for operating 2010s media brands like Bustle and Elite Daily, tells WIRED.

Much like those two digital media companies once did, Polymarket has put its own spin on engagement via rage-baiting. What’s the 2026 version of an ill-advised xoJane personal essay riling up Twitter? It looks an awful lot like the podcaster Amanda Hirsch getting eviscerated on TikTok for creating paid content for Polymarket promoting how people could wager on the outcome of the Lindsay Clancy trial. The backlash was severe enough that Hirsch, who is another one of the What Are the Odds? hosts, apologized.

There are obvious advantages to these companies going all-in on media strategy. For starters, it turbocharges brand awareness, doubling as marketing. For companies that like to talk about how they might be used to protect investments, creating a potential revenue generator separate from trading fees is itself a way to diversify risk. It also helps the markets shape their own narratives.

In a January 2026 announcement about its decision to partner with Polymarket, Wall Street Journal publisher and Dow Jones CEO Almar Latour described the prediction market as a “rapidly growing source of real-time insight into collective beliefs about future events.” It did not mention that the company’s flagship product remains banned in the US. (Polymarket now has an app that is federally regulated in the United States called Polymarket US, though it offers a narrower range of markets than its original decentralized product.)

Not every media outlet is embracing these markets as a potential partner or peer. The New York Times recently scuttled a potential partnership between Kalshi and its sports-focused subsidiary, The Athletic, after pushback from its union.

Still, things aren’t slowing down. Earlier this month, Polymarket launched a group-chat feature called Squads, with the idea that people wagering on its platforms want to socialize and strategize together. The recognition goes both ways. As NPR first reported, Meta considered buying Kalshi and later discussed launching its own internal prediction market. The social media juggernaut sniffing around the prediction market space isn’t an indication that the company is hungry to get into trading or gambling—it’s more evidence that this is part of the future of media. Meta, despite its best efforts, remains a digital media company, and it’s savvy enough to see that these markets are increasingly part of how people use the internet.

As these companies keep expanding their reach, their media maneuvers will only grow more important. There may well be other efforts to refine editorial products in the near future, even a renewed attempt to hire journalists.
